opus-5.5.text:
Right now the report is the most visible part of a scout, but it was never the point. When someone sets up a scout, they're really saying, "I care about this thing in the world, and I want to know when something changes so I can act on it." The report is just the first step of that.

So the natural evolution is closing that loop. Today a scout might tell you that the flight you've been watching dropped in price, or that a restaurant you like opened up reservations for Friday. The next step is the scout saying, "Here's the change, and do you want me to book it?" Eventually, for things you've given it permission to handle, it just does it and tells you afterward. We think of that as a spectrum, from monitoring to recommending to acting. Where a given task sits depends on how much trust has been built and how high the stakes are.

The other piece is that scouts get better as they learn about you. A first-time scout is fairly literal: you told it what to look for, and it looks for that. Over time it should pick up on what you actually click on, what you ignore, and what you follow up on. Then it can tune what counts as worth interrupting you for. A lot of the value is in what it chooses *not* to tell you.

I'm also excited about scouts working together. If you have one tracking your kid's school announcements and another tracking your calendar, there's real value in them noticing that a schedule change conflicts with something you already have planned. Today those feel like separate streams of information. They should feel more like one assistant that understands your life.

Underneath all of this, what we're building toward is a world where you're not the one constantly refreshing tabs and checking things. You delegate the attention part to something that's always on, and you get to spend your own attention on the decisions that actually need you. Reports were a good way to start because they're low-risk and easy to trust. But the long-term vision is much more about agents that act on your behalf on the web.

r001.rationale: It describes scouts moving from reporting changes to recommending or taking action, first asking for approval and later acting when authorized.

r002.rationale: It does not mention scouting APIs, webhooks, or building custom workflows.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish tasks that end when a goal is achieved from ongoing monitoring without a natural endpoint.

r004.rationale: It says scouts should learn from what users click, ignore, and follow up on, then use that behavior to tune what they report or interrupt users about.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that reports are really just the first, most legible form factor for what a scout is doing. Right now a scout is something you set up once, you tell it what you care about, and it goes out and watches the web for you continuously and comes back when something relevant happens. The output happens to be a report, or a notification, because that's the easiest thing for a person to consume and the easiest thing for us to evaluate.

But the underlying capability is really persistent attention. It's an agent that holds onto an intent over time, and that's actually the harder and more interesting thing. So the natural evolution is that the scout stops being a thing that tells you something changed, and starts being a thing that does something about it. If I have a scout watching for a particular apartment listing or a flight price or a competitor's job postings, the next step isn't a nicer summary, it's that it drafts the inquiry, or books the thing within parameters I've set, or kicks off a downstream workflow. The report becomes a byproduct, or maybe just a log of what the agent did on your behalf.

The second axis is that scouts become more collaborative and more composable. Today each scout is fairly independent. But a lot of what people actually want is a scout that feeds another scout, or a small team of them that collectively maintain a picture of something, like a market or a research area, and keep it up to date. That starts to look less like alerts and more like a living model of the world that you can query.

And the third thing, which I think is underrated, is that the scout should get better at understanding what you actually meant. People are bad at specifying what they care about up front. So the agent should be learning from what you click on, what you ignore, what you follow up on, and gradually tightening its own sense of relevance. That feedback loop is where a lot of the value is going to come from. The report is the surface. The persistence, the action, and the learning are what we're really building.

r001.rationale: The response describes scouts taking actions, including booking within user-set parameters, but does not clearly say users approve those actions.

r002.rationale: It does not mention scouting APIs or webhooks for building custom workflows.

r003.rationale: It describes continuous monitoring but does not distinguish tasks that end when a goal is achieved from tasks with no natural endpoint.

r004.rationale: It says the scout should learn from what users click, ignore, or follow up on to improve its sense of relevance, describing feedback shaping later outputs.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting shift is from scouts telling you what happened to helping you figure out what to do next. A report is useful, but you still have to read it, connect it to your goals, and decide whether something needs your attention.

You can imagine a scout becoming a more ongoing collaborator. It notices something, brings you the relevant context, and says, “This might matter for what you’re working on. Would you like me to dig deeper?” And as you give it feedback, it gets a better sense of what’s useful to you and when to interrupt.

Over time, that could extend to taking actions within boundaries you’ve set. But the key is that it understands enough about your intent to make those actions useful, and you have visibility into what it’s doing and control over the consequential decisions.

r001.rationale: The response describes scouts eventually taking actions within user-set boundaries and gives users visibility and control, but it does not clearly say those actions require the user's approval.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention scouting APIs, webhooks, or custom workflows built on scout reports.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish goal-based scouting tasks from ongoing monitoring without a natural endpoint.

r004.rationale: It says user feedback helps the scout learn what is useful and when to interrupt, but does not clearly identify feedback on reports as shaping subsequent reports.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reports are a starting point. The more interesting direction is for scouts to become persistent collaborators that understand what you care about, keep an eye on how things are changing, and bring something to your attention when it matters. Rather than giving you another document to read, they might say, “This connects to the question you were exploring last week,” or, “Something has changed that could affect your decision.”

And then you can imagine moving from surfacing information to helping you act on it—following up on a question, exploring an alternative, or coordinating a next step, with the right level of human involvement. The challenge is figuring out when to be proactive and when to stay out of the way. That requires understanding your context and preferences, and earning your trust over time.

r001.rationale: It describes scouts helping users act and mentions human involvement, but does not clearly say those actions happen with the user's approval.

r002.rationale: It does not mention scouting APIs, webhooks, or custom workflows built on scout reports.

r004.rationale: It mentions learning user preferences and earning trust, but does not say users can give feedback on reports to shape later reports.
